utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I see that it has been possible for all accused to be present today, which is reassuring. Are we ready to continue -- oh, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to give to the Chamber a brief update as to where we are with regard to Mr. Bala's health. He was at the hospital yesterday. He was checked, apparently, with regard specifically to cardiac function and was cleared for those purposes and then returned to the Detention Unit. Approximately 7.00 last night he once again was experiencing, from what I understand his reporting to me, extreme pain; requested the assistance of medical staff, which did not arrive. He is in better shape today than he was before, and I have discussed with him whether or not he is in a position and a condition to proceed. Because quite frankly, my looking at him, he does not look particularly well to me and I have seen him over a period of time and I have noticed that on occasion he manifests his physical disability quite obviously. He has told me he does not feel particularly good today. He has also told me that he can carry on and wishes to carry on because he does not wish to delay the proceedings or have anyone feel at any point in time that he is trying to delay these proceedings and is quite concerned about a perception someone or some peoples might have in that regard. I've told him that if he is comfortable proceeding today, I'm willing to proceed. I've asked him in the event that if anything comes up such that he is experiencing any further pain or further discomfort, that he immediately notify me so that we can attend to the matter immediately. I don't know if this is the appropriate time to raise the issue again. We have previously discussed a comprehensive medical examination for this gentleman. This is not the first time he has been in crisis. Something is going on. I am not a doctor. And I would certainly never wish to take the position that I know what is going on, because I don't. There is something going on in this man that is a bit more profound than normal and we are not reaching an understanding of what it is. I think it would be prudent for the Trial Chamber, if you feel it appropriate, to order another comprehensive medical examination of Mr. Bala to see if we can get to the bottom of this for many, many reasons, not the least of which is his health as well as the ability to make sure that the case which he wishes to proceed in an expeditious manner is able to do so. Other than that, I have very little to report with regard to that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I will make some inquiries to see whether there is in the view of those presently responsible for his care any reason to follow up your suggestion. Beyond that, the position that you have indicated is very much what the Chamber would think appropriate. Clearly, if your client feels significantly unwell, that should be drawn to the Chamber's attention. Otherwise, if we're able to continue, that is desirable. The -- your client should not at any time feel that he should not draw attention to his health out of concern that it may be thought he's trying to delay the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- if I may briefly just add on this issue just one piece of information, which is that this issue has come up before and in fact it is my understanding that it's either in 2003 or it may have been in 2004 there was a comprehensive medical examination ordered for this very reason. It was done and the results were made available and the case proceeded. Obviously one's health can change over time. It's been -- it has -- there has been a passage of time and so perhaps it is appropriate to do such an examination again. But I thought it should be made clear that this issue has been addressed in the past and such exams have been done. It may have been before Mr. Guy-Smith started representing Mr. Bala; I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly before this Chamber was appointed to try this case, if that has occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was indeed before this Chamber was appointed to try the case. And Mr. Whiting is correct; other examinations have been done. There is what I understand to be some unspecified aetiology, although all parties seem to acknowledge that something is amiss. As we all know, the science of medicine is somewhat inexact, although we wish it not to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We won't compare it with law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, not at all. I would never do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the present witness is out of court at my request. It is, as I understand it, the case that Mr. Whiting has finished his examination-in-chief of the witness. I was able to indicate to him this morning a matter that I wish to raise before cross-examination began and I should like to raise that in a moment. But first may I place on record the position regarding Mr. Limaj, and Mr. Mansfield. And may I thank the Court for its involvement and help backstage this morning. Nothing runs smooth as far as Mr. Mansfield's other case is concerned and yet again he was confronted with yet another sick juror. However I am able to tell you at the Central Criminal Court this morning he concluded his closing speech and he is on his way back to this city as we speak. Your Honours, I think I shall be the only Defence counsel this afternoon asking Mr. Qeriqi questions. Even if I went very slowly indeed, I do not think I could take up the time it would take between now and Mr. Mansfield's potential arrival -- subject to snow -- which is at about into this building something at about just before 6.00. I know in those circumstances, and I know Mr. Limaj is very grateful, as I understand it the Court would not be overconcerned if Mr. Qeriqi went over until tomorrow to enable Mr. Mansfield himself to cross-examine him should that be necessary. And I know Mr. Whiting and I discussed whether he, Qeriqi, could be interposed after the next witness has begun and for a variety of reasons, all of which I sympathise and I know the Court does, that was not thought by counsel to be desirable. With those pieces of information and thanks to the Court, that is the position as far as Mr. Mansfield is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Topolski. Although we all appreciate it's unfortunate, it would I think be in the best interest of Mr. Mansfield's client if Mr. Mansfield had time to draw his breath after arriving and time to become familiar with what has happened in the course of the evidence and your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For that reason, don't feel under any obligation to hasten slowly. Get on with it and we'll enjoy the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I hope the phrase "get on with it" and "Topolski" might be becoming synonymous in the Court's mind, but I don't push for an answer to that question. Your Honours, may I raise the matter I wanted to raise at the conclusion of Mr. Qeriqi's evidence in-chief, and it's unusual to raise it. It's unique in this case thus far to raise it, but I do so and I should indicate straightaway what it is. What I seek from Mr. Whiting on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor is an indication as to what the Prosecutor's position is with regard to this witness's evidence thus far. Of course one appreciates and understands well that ultimately these are matters for the Trial Chamber when it comes to consider guilt or innocence of these accused, but, Your Honour, it impinges on the subject matter of some of my cross-examination. I indicate now how, we submit, this arises uniquely with regards to Qeriqi. First of all, there has not been and there will not be any application for him to be regarded as a hostile witness. Second of all, certainly in the jurisdiction from which I practice and I know from which Your Honours do, too, and I know -- I believe also Mr. Whiting's, the concept of a witness being called by the Prosecution as a witness of truth is a concept that holds good for all these jurisdictions and certainly for this one. The next point is this: that one recognises certainly when the Prosecution and perhaps even the Defence call a witness, it might be the position that one is not necessarily calling a witness who one thinks as prosecuting or Defence counsel is giving honest, truthful, and reliable answers in relation to all matters, but only some. Here the situation with regard to this witness is qualitatively different, we submit. And that difference generates the need, as we perceive it to be, for Mr. Whiting, to a degree at least, nail his colours to the mast. And these are the reasons why, we submit, it arises. First of all, this witness is and for all we know remains a suspect. He was clearly told so in the opening lines of his interview -- at which Mr. Whiting, I add in parentheses, was present -- when he was interviewed by the ICTY. It is clearly the case indicated in evidence before you that he submitted to a summons to appear for interview as a suspect and he submitted to a subpoena to appear before this Court. I certainly would propose to ask him whether he still believes himself to be a suspect in this case. Whether or not Mr. Whiting is prepared to indicate whether he is still a suspect or whether any indication has been given to him that he is no longer a suspect we shall wait for Mr. Whiting's response. The second matter is this: that other witnesses, and I pick one example as an obvious one and we're in open session so I shall simply refer to him by pseudonym, L-07, has given evidence of an interrogation by people at which this witness was said to be present, an interrogation that this witness was invited to deal with yesterday, in relation to which he gave answers regarding the carriage of beer and cigarettes to, as it were, both sides of the argument in Kosovo at once. What was not put to him, of course, was the very serious allegation that L-07 made that at that interview L-07's teeth were knocked out by a rifle butt; in other words that this witness, in a position either as a perpetrator of a criminal act or in a position of a command responsibility in relation to a criminal act, was directly implicated. One remembers clearly the tone in which Mr. Whiting perfectly properly but firmly put to this witness in-chief a number of names of disappeared and dead. And the unspoken allegation behind each and every one of those was plainly that this witness knew or knows or might have known of more than he was prepared to say. No application for hostility was made. In effect, he denies or continues to deny any matter that could link him to criminal behaviour. Your Honours, this is not a public inquiry. Neutrality on this by the Prosecution is not, in our submission, an option. We are entitled to know the case we are obliged to meet and I am entitled to know how to cross-examine this witness, given what Mr. Whiting's response to this submission, if any, is or may be. May I just give two examples of why I say it is relevant to my forthcoming cross-examination. This witness gave evidence yesterday regarding what he understood to be my client's position in Lapusnik. I'll put it no higher than this at the moment because the Court is never blessed with the texts of interviews that have preceded these proceedings. Let us put it neutrally and say that contrasts with answers he gave in interview to Mr. Whiting and others. I use the word "contrasts" in its proper sense. Whether I go down that route or not depends to a degree at least, I can assure the Court, on how Mr. Whiting responds to this submission, if invited to do so. And the second matter is this, and I've already touched upon it by giving one example of it, and it is not the only example, the position of Ramadan Behluli is another example. But this Court has heard allegations by other witnesses regarding this witness's conduct. And it could be thought that in the spirit of fairness that if those allegations are to hang in the air, this witness ought to be given an opportunity of dealing with them. That is an area in relation to which I seek the guidance of the Court in response to my submissions now because I want to know whether, as it were, from my point of view that is an appropriate and/or safe area in which to go. Of course matters of safety are matters entirely for me; I appreciate that. But, Your Honours, this is the situation we face as I have said uniquely I think in the case thus far, and therefore it seem to us to be both necessary and appropriate to raise this matter now. Of course, if the Court's view is: Well, this is all a matter for the Court at the end of the day and I must take my own course, well then of course I shall abide by that and do so. But I hope the Court can see that there are particular potential difficulties here. And it is well worth, in our submission, airing them now, given this situation than leaving it until it may be too late. Your Honour, forgive me for taking a little time developing that, but that is the matter upon which I seek the Court's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will join in the remarks made thus far by Mr. Topolski. I have one second thought, but that also depends on the manner in which Mr. Whiting responds to the issue presented in the event that you're going to invite him to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is quite resistant at this point, in the middle of a witness's testimony, to begin a process of evaluating that witness's testimony and offering the Prosecution's views or opinions or judgement about what parts might be true, what parts might not be true, what parts ultimately the Prosecution will rely on, what parts it will not rely on. There's several reasons for this, and some have been touched on by Mr. Topolski. The first is that it's not up to the Prosecution but up to the Court to make the evaluation about the witness's evidence, about whether to accept the evidence in whole or in part. And therefore, even if the Prosecution were to put forward its position on the witness, I wouldn't expect the Court would do the same, and therefore Mr. Topolski would be in the same -- in really no better position in terms of figuring out where to go on his cross-examination. Ultimately it's going to be the Court's judgement that will matter, not our judgement. So Mr. Topolski will have to keep that in mind. The second point is that this evidence, as with all evidence in this case, has to be evaluated in light of all the evidence that comes in. Of course it may be possible during the case to make certain kind of snap judgements about evidence, but ultimately witnesses -- their evidence, documents, whatever comes in as evidence has to be evaluated in light of everything at the end, and that is the appropriate time to -- for the Prosecution to make submissions about which evidence it intends to rely on and for -- of course for the Defence to do so the same and for the Court to make its evaluation. As a general matter, I think it's -- it frequently happens in -- it will happen, I expect, in this trial if it hasn't already happened and it happens in every trial in this building that witnesses will tell the truth about certain matters and on other matters will not be accurate, either intentionally or unintentionally. In particular, witnesses may be less than candid about their own involvement in matters or the involvement of their side in a conflict in matters. I think that is common. And in fact, it's addressed in paragraph 7 at the very beginning of the Strugar judgement of this Chamber, the fact that witnesses are truthful on some matters, not on other matters; exaggerate certain issues, minimise other issues. And it's up to the Court to weigh all of that and to make a determination about whether to accept the witnesses' evidence in whole or in part. Now, Mr. Topolski in his submission stated that it is to be -- I think he accepted this principle and said -- I don't have the line in front of me, but said it's quite common for the Prosecution or the Defence to call witnesses who will be truthful on some matters and not truthful on other matters, but then he seeks to distinguish this witness as a unique situation and made a few points on that which I will address. The first point was that the witness was interviewed as a suspect and the question is: Is he still a suspect or not? On this matter I see one -- one point where I should respond, and that is: The witness was told that he was a suspect. If he -- at some point he received a different piece of information or other evaluation of his status, I could accept that that would -- could affect his evidence, and that is something that I would -- I would be under an obligation to disclose. That has not occurred. There has been no such information given to the witness. And there -- on that -- on that specific point I think it's proper for the Prosecution to be required to disclose if a witness has been informed that his status in that regard has changed. However, whether he is a suspect or not, what's going to happen with him, those are matters -- aside from what he has been told, because that might affect his evidence, what his status is in the mind of the Prosecution I don't think is a relevant matter. The second point is that Mr. Topolski said that -- or the certainly doesn't distinguish this witness from any other witness who might have involvement or have allegations of involvement in activities and who might come and testify in this courtroom. The second point is that Mr. Topolski asserts that the witness's evidence about his client's position is different in the prior -- in his prior interview. Well, that's -- well, that's -- that certainly doesn't distinguish him from other witnesses who come into this courtroom and may tell the truth about some matters and not other matters or be truthful entirely, and that's something that Mr. Topolski can explore on cross-examination. That's a proper subject for cross-examination. And I don't see any impediment to that. The third point is that there -- Mr. Topolski said that the Court has heard allegations against this witness and that the witness should be given an opportunity to deal with them. That is precisely what I sought to do at the end of my direct examination, is confront the witness with the allegations that -- and the evidence that have been made against him and give him an opportunity to deal with them and let the Court evaluate, in light of all the other evidence, whether it believes that the witness is being truthful in his responses on those subjects. Now, there may be -- I tried to cover the ground as thoroughly as I could, asking both general and specific questions. It may be that there are specific allegations that I did not directly put to the witness. Mr. Topolski has identified one about -- regarding L-07, but I certainly -- I haven't reviewed the transcript on that inquiry about L-07, but it's my memory that I covered that incident pretty thoroughly and with both general questions and specific questions. And the witness was quite clear in his testimony about that incident. So in my submission, there is nothing that distinguishes this witness from any other witness that will come and testify in this courtroom and that should require the Prosecution at this stage in the proceeding to begin a mid-course evaluation of the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position is clear that the Prosecution in calling in witness and leading evidence from him does so on the basis that it will advance him as a witness whose evidence could, at least in part, be accepted by the Chamber. It is not the position, as we understand it, that by calling the witness the Prosecution is advancing thereby the proposition that all of his evidence is evidence of a witness of truth. I would think that the matters raised by Mr. Topolski are really indications of the degree to which some of the matters in this witness's case are more evident and of greater force than is the case with many other witnesses. There are significant allegations to be found elsewhere in the evidence against this witness. There are other issues concerning his own involvement in certain matters, to mention just some aspects. The degree, though, does not appear to the Chamber as affecting the underlying principle. The witness has been called on the basis I have suggested by the Prosecution. The Prosecution has canvassed with him some aspects of these significant allegations to be found elsewhere in the evidence. The effect of his evidence, as the Chamber understands it on those matters, is to deny that he has had any involvement of the type suggested by the other evidence, and that appears to have been the position he takes without qualification in respect of any of the allegations. If the Prosecution had a clear and firm position at this point, it could have been a matter of considerable convenience and assistance to the Defence to have that position indicated. The Prosecution, however, indicates that the task of evaluating the extent to which it may in the end rely upon the evidence of this witness in support of its case is one that in the circumstances it would prefer to deal with in the ordinary way, that is after there has been an opportunity to evaluate the totality of the evidence. The Chamber does not feel that the circumstances warrant any intervention to alter that position, which it seems to be one which is correct in principle and open to the Prosecution to take as a matter of fairness in the conduct of the trial. For those reasons, Mr. Topolski, we will not call specifically on the Prosecution to indicate its position further, but I think that you may now see well that it certainly will perhaps be picking and choosing over the field of this witness's evidence at the end of its case. So I suggest wherever you see a need, you should explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could we have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Qeriqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will see that fortunately all accused are now able to be present so that we can continue with your evidence. If I could remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Whiting, is there anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that event then, counsel for the Defence will now ask questions of you, Mr. Qeriqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I -- if you allow me, I would like to have it translated in my language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The equipment needs to be tuned to the correct channel, it seems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you getting me in Albanian now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything you want me to repeat of what's been said or did you understand it enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I understood it because I already stated that I know four other languages besides my language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you then, Mr. Qeriqi. The Defence counsel will now perhaps have some questions for you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Qeriqi, I represent Isak Musliu and I would like to ask you some questions this afternoon, if I may.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: When you attended for an interview in April of 2003 with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, you did so as a suspect. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't know if that is correct or not, but this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, today as you sit here in front of us do you believe you are still a suspect?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone has a right to suspect, but I think they have no longer this right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Have you ever received any communication of any kind in any form from the Office of the Prosecutor that indicates you are no longer regarded as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I don't know what you mean by any communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Any letter, telephone call, fax, text, e-mail, anything of that kind at all from the Office of the Prosecutor telling you that you are no longer regarded as a suspect. Have you received anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not received anything in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. In the interview with the Office of the Prosecutor and indeed I think yesterday, you referred to joining the war as a KLA soldier and hiding your identity. And I just want to ask you briefly about that. Your pseudonym, your nom de guerre, was Luani. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And would I be right in suggesting, Mr. Qeriqi, that you and many, many others took that -- a pseudonym for two reasons: predominantly to protect your own identity from the Serbs. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to protect myself but also to protect the families at the relatives, because at that time the then-government if it knew that someone was against it he would take it out on the entire family, either by imprisoning them or ransacking their houses in the middle of the night, maltreating them and so on. That was the reason why we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that answer in such detail, because I was going to suggest that was the second of the two reasons why you would want to protect your identity, to protect your family, and you've dealt with it. I want to now ask you some questions about Germany and your time in Germany because it is there, Mr. Qeriqi, I suggest that you met with and became a friend of Isak Musliu, my client. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You may remember that Isak Musliu was staying in a place called Degendorf. Do you recollect the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Degendorf, not then, but when he came near my place, near Barkenberg. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you know that he was a member of a local karate club and played football, too?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I met him I realised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You became in your words yesterday inseparable. I'll use another: You became close friends. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at a later phase. When you ask me later when we became friends, I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'll come to that. I want to deal with your very first meeting. I suggest that he was working in an agricultural job in a village called Arnhofen near the town of Neuseddin in Germany. It was a cold day. He was working in the fields with two cousins and a man brought some tea in a thermos; that man was you. Do you remember this, Mr. Qeriqi?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't buy the tea. My family was close by, so I brought the tea to them because this is where I lived. I had my wife and a son there. And the place they were working was very close to my family. And I had -- I felt pleased to serve some of my compatriots, at least to give them some tea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think I can go through this part of the events swiftly. These are parts of my client's case; I want to put them to you for your comment. You started working together in an organisation that helped with security for gatherings held to support the KLA, working with an increasing number of those who would volunteer to participate in meetings and the organisation of meetings for what was to become the KLA. Do you agree, Mr. Qeriqi?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. It was a pleasure when we got together. All those persons who were involved in this organisation or movement, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to move on and deal with matters chronologically. I want to deal with the time when it became the case that you and he and ten others crossed or left Germany en route for Kosovo. First of all, Mr. Qeriqi, you made an application, you told us the day before yesterday, for permission to go. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I wanted to return to Kosovo. I wanted to leave Germany; that's why we made the application because we wanted to join the friend, the comrades, to defend our territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Forgive me. I'm sorry for interrupting you. You kindly provided -- you kindly provided to Mr. Whiting and his team a copy of that application, which I'm not going to put in front of you but I've had it translated together with a list of names attached to it. I just want to ask you this: To whom did you make that application?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made this application in Aargau with the members of LPK because these were the persons who were dealing with this affair and they undertook to do the organisation, more than the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The list of names of 12 include Isak Musliu and yourself and ten others. Would I be right in suggesting, Mr. Qeriqi, that it was the martyrdom, as you would call it, in early March of the Jashari family, specifically on the 5th of March, that was the event that drove you to decide the time had come to return to Kosovo. Would I be right in suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would be very right. Not only the family of Adem Jashari, but the Serbs had started to bring pressure on us at an earlier phase. I don't want to take your time to dwell on that and explain why it was not only myself, Isak Musliu, and others that were involved, but all the Albanians who could do so were willing to return and fight to defend our lands and to uphold the identity of -- our national identity as Albanians, to defend our children, our women who were powerless, weak. So this was not the case only with a single family, but it was to serve a broader interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't for one moment diminish the significance of the event; I was actually more interested in the date that this journey to Kosova from Germany for you and your comrades starts, does it not, in early March, Mr. Qeriqi. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In March we have taken part in some rallies. I stress that we had applied even earlier, but it was in March that we travelled. I'm not sure about the date. I think it must have been the end of March or early April, but I think more so at the end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: For the most part, that journey you took, you took, I suggest, with Isak Musliu -- I'm not going to go into the detail of it, but you certainly spent, did you not, a few days, about a week, in Tirana, in Albania? And you were, were you not, Mr. Qeriqi, in effect the leader of this group returning to Kosovo. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was the leader, but in Tirana there were other leaders as well who helped us to get back into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you go then to a place - and you'll forgive, sir, and others, my mispronunciation - to place called Kukes to a house where you were given uniforms and weapons? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't take the uniforms in Kukes. We took them somewhere else. We went to Krume then. From that place we entered Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. Perhaps the name of the village doesn't much matter. Crossing into Kosovo I suggest you did as a group, about somewhere at the end of March of 1998, you went to a house across the border. You met a man called Abedin Rexha and Ilaz Kodra and you discovered -- by which I mean you, Musliu, and others -- that the KLA then was not as organised as you perhaps thought it might be. Now, I put that all of a piece. I hope you followed what I said. I can break it up if you wish me to, but do you agree with all of that or disagree with any of it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding Abedin and Ilaz, we met somewhere else, in Germany, not in this place where we cross into Kosova. Maybe you have misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, it's my fault if I have got that wrong. The rest of what I suggested to you, does that accord with your recollection of events, particularly, Mr. Qeriqi, the suggestion that I'm putting that you discovered, all of you, that things were in no sense organised when you got to Kosovo as far as the KLA was concerned. In particular, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the names are the same, the ones I mentioned yesterday; only the place is different, is wrong actually, because we had met these two other persons in Germany. When we arrived there, we met them in Likovc, not in a house somewhere else. It was in Likovc that we met these two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I would like to show you the photograph you were shown a couple of days ago, P153, please with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be put on the ELMO. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As we look at the photograph together, if you look to your right -- to your left, rather, Mr. Qeriqi, you can see it on the screen there -- or is it on the screen in front of you as well?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Looking at the photograph, the gentleman kneeling to the right of the photograph is Qerqizi, is he not, that is Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He has in that photograph, does he not, a significant beard that became longer and fuller as the spring and summer wore on, didn't it? And you can answer that because you certainly saw him up until the end of May in Lapusnik. Do you agree with me that his beard grew and grew?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the beard grew. But at that time he did have a beard and he resembled Qerqiz Topulli, a hero of the past who fought for the national question and that was from where he got the pseudonym. Of course a beard would grow with the passage of time. I don't know what to say about that. I don't have any other thing -- anything else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, you've answered the question; that's all I require of you, Mr. Qeriqi. The significance of the beard is for others, not for you; don't worry about it. Let's move on, please. I want to deal with your dealings with Qerqizi and in particular your dealings with him in Lapusnik. Your first visit to Lapusnik was on the 9th of May. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And if I eve understood your evidence correctly, you participate in the fighting on that day; you leave within 24 hours; and you return for your second visit on the 29th of May and you don't go back again during the war. Now, have I understood your evidence correctly or not as far as you and Lapusnik are concerned?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you have understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's deal with it in the order in which it happened; it will be easier to follow. First of all, the decision to go to Lapusnik at all on the 9th of May was a decision taken by individuals, was it not? No one ordered anyone there. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said yesterday we were in Klecke. We heard the shots and we left Klecke and went there to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Qeriqi, please don't worry about what you've already said. If anyone here thinks I'm wasting time, I'll be corrected by the Judges. If you would be good enough to answer my questions; I'm trying to focus them as best I can. You were not ordered to go. You heard the shooting yourselves and you all decided, those of you who wanted to, that you needed to go to Lapusnik to help the village. Am I right or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our struggle was a liberation struggle. There are many cases; I have not touched on all of them. In some instances people just joined us. They had a gun, hunting gun, or anything. We were going to the front, and people just joined our ranks. As I said, it was a voluntary war; that is a fact, common knowledge. Like the case was with all those persons who wanted to go to Kosova, some of them didn't make it. So nobody dealt with them after that. Everybody who wanted came -- did so voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If I were to show you a map of Lapusnik, an aerial photograph, would you be able to identify where it was you fought on the 9th of May or not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may describe it in words without a map if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did the place you fought have a name?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained the day before yesterday that we arrived there rather late. After the APC was in flames, the group that I was leading arrived there rather late. The Serbs were retreating by that time, and the APC was there in a place -- near a place called Guri where even today there is a flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Today the word guri meaning rock has the red two-headed eagle flag flying from it, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two-headed eagle is our national symbol and it has its significance to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You left Lapusnik that same day, the 9th of May, and you were not to return again for another 20 days, as you've already agreed. I want to ask you then about your return on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Wait for the question, Mr. Qeriqi. I haven't asked you one yet.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It's all right. Again, was it a case of you being ordered back to Lapusnik on the 29th or a decision you and others made to go and assist the village again? Which was it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that day I was in Kroimire and we heard the shots. I took three other comrades and we went together in a neighbourhood of Komorane which is in the -- closer to Lapusnik; that's where we took up positions. And from that place we attacked the Serbs. They fired back at us with heavy weapons, with all sorts of weapons, in the direction of Lapusnik. It was only an assistance that we wanted to render them. This is what we did every time we heard shots. We felt we had to go there and help because we were fighting under the same emblem. We were all members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you meet with Isak Musliu, Qerqizi, on the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you become aware that his position within Lapusnik had changed between the 9th and the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I have no knowledge about that. I don't know whether it changed or not because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let me put to you the specific change that occurred to see if you'd heard anything about this. Somewhere around the 14th of May he was asked by other soldiers in Lapusnik to become the leader of one of - and I underline the words "one of" - the KLA units in Lapusnik. Did you hear that at all before you went back on the 29th?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated that Isak might have been a leader of some unit, a squad probably or a platoon; this is what I believed. But I have never said for sure because there was no way how I should know. That was my idea and I think it coincides with what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I only want to deal with knowledge that you had yourself at the time. Did you know anything at all about the organisation and structure of the KLA in Lapusnik or were you - and I don't mean the word rudely - ignorant about the way they organised themselves? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ignorant of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I want to ask you another aspect of organisation and I want to move away from Lapusnik in doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're moving to another topic, I think it may be convenient --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was a short session from your point of view because we had some preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, forgive me; I completely lost track of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume then at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Topolski -- oh, you -- cross-examination will conclude very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very successfully, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Qeriqi, I just have a few more questions for you. As I say, I want to try and deal with things continuing in date order. We dealt with the 9th of May and the 29th of May. You also gave evidence two days ago regarding fighting on the 14th of June. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you explain again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. You told us about some fighting in your area of Carraleve on the 14th of June of 1998. Do you remember telling Their Honours about that two days ago when you gave evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I gave evidence the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's right. You told us you were leading that battle and you indicated to us the weaponry that was at your disposal. I want to ask you about one particular weapon. You told us that the largest weapon you had was the hand-held rocket launcher. Mr. Qeriqi, do you mean to tell the Court that there was only one of those on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was that 150-millimetres hand-held rocket launcher that was the biggest one. There were a Kalashnikovs, automatic rifles; snipers, we had, too, some very old snipers; and in some cases people fought with hunting guns. What I meant was our weapons were more powerful than the enemy weapons. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did the 150-millimetre hand-held rocket launcher have to be shared between units because there was only one of them?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So if - and I'll just use this as an example, not the names that were the case - if unit called number 1 needed the rocket-propelled grenade launcher, someone would have to go and get it from somebody else. Was that the position in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes we used it in Zborce, sometimes in Carraleve, and even in Blinaje, not somewhere else as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'll move from weaponry to equipment. You told us the day before yesterday dealing with this same period that you didn't have a radio, you used couriers. Mr. Qeriqi, for how long were you without a radio; or put another way, can you tell us when you first got use of a radio during the war?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my unit we didn't have one. For the first time I used a radio in the fighting in Koshare.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what month that took place, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took place in - as far as I remember, I stressed it the day before yesterday - in April 1999. There were many radios there. It was a regular army. The means were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Qeriqi, do you mean to tell the Tribunal that you as a local commander did not have the use of a radio throughout the year of 1998? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the use of a radio at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on through the calendar, I want to deal with an event, if you can recollect it, on the 24th of July of 1998. Mr. Qeriqi, we know from other evidence in this case uncontested that Lapusnik fell at around this time during the course of the summer offensive by the Serbs. I want to ask you about a particular place and a particular date and see if you can help us. I suggest that you and Shukri Buja were near a village or outside of a village called Fustica at around July 1998. I'm being very specific about this. First of all, can you remember being at a place called Fustica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall to be at home. We went there to help the war in Fushtice, but until we went there -- I don't remember about Shukri. I remember we went there with some soldiers. But when we arrived there the enemy forces had taken over the place so we were unable to penetrate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can bring it back to life for you, as it were. I suggest apart from Shukri Buja also met Qerqizi there and Qerqizi had just come from Rahovec. You're nodding your head. Do you remember this, Mr. Qeriqi?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Qerqiz was with another group. I was with another when we went to help Fustica. This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry to press it. I haven't had quite an answer to my question. I'm trying to be specific with details. If you can't help me, say so. I'm suggesting that Qerqizi may have told you that he'd just come back from Rahovec and that he met you and Shukri Buja and in fact he then decided to attack Serb forces in Fustica. Now do you remember any of this or not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Qerqiz and many others, Voglushi, were there, because our aim was to prevent the Serb forces from entering Rusinoc but we were unable to go into Fustice before the war. We had some places outside Fustice, between Fustice and Rusinoc village. This was the place from where we fired, but we were unable to enter Fustice. It is true Qerqiz was there. He might have told me what you have mentioned, but I don't remember now. If he had said so, then it's true. But if you mentioned -- when you mentioned Fustice I wanted to point out that we were unable to enter there and we fired from those positions between Fustice and Rusinoc. But there were many groups there. I had some five or six people with me and then I returned to Carraleve because I had to be there in case of a possible attack there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like just your help with a geography lesson, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could the witness be given P6 from map 1, the large map book. Perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO because I'm going to ask you to point one or two places out to us, if you would be so kind, Mr. Qeriqi. I want to have it so the witness can see Lapusnik as well, so can we come back. Your Honours, I'm sorry, my screen is virtually unseeable, so I'm having a little difficulty. Have we got Lapusnik on the map? Down, please, Mr. Harvey says. Can you bring that down south on the ELMO. A little more. That's it. Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Qeriqi, could you use the map to your left please, sir, if you wouldn't mind and could you use the pointer because I want you to point out one or two places to us. First of all, you'll see Lapusnik, it's within a red square. If you look to your left, look at the map on the machine, if you wouldn't mind, Mr. Qeriqi.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: With the usher's help I want you to look at that one. Thank you. You see Lapusnik. First of all, we've just been talking together, you and I, about Fustica. Can you point to Fustica on this map, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how long it would take by car to get to Lapusnik from Fustica, approximately.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to tell because there's no straight road. You had to come from Nekovce and from Nekovce to Bajice. To come back here -- I am unable to explain. I may make a mistake because I've never used that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: All right. I was going to ask you if you've ever done the journey, but never mind. Can you show us Klecka on this map, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Have you ever done the journey from Klecka to Lapusnik yourself by car?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have done the journey from Klecke to Lapusnik, but never by car only by -- on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: How long did it take you on foot, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took me a long time, maybe two or three hours. I may not be very accurate because I didn't measure the time actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No. Finally this, because you've mentioned it just now, can you show us the village of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a village; it is a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the town of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it here in this map. I see only an arrow that goes in the direction, that is the road going in the direction of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it here. Rahovec is very far from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Have you -- well, I was going to ask you: Have you ever done the journey by road or by car or by foot from Rahovec to Lapusnik? Have you ever done that journey yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have done the journey only after the war when we went to play football with the football team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you give the Court some idea, please, of how long it might take you to drive from Rahovec to Lapusnik, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you drive fast I think it would take you one and a half hours, one, one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't need the map anymore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you I hope very few questions, Mr. Qeriqi, regarding structure and organisation of the KLA. Again with the assistance of the usher I wonder if you could have put back in front of you P155. This you were good enough to produce to us two days ago, Mr. Qeriqi, and it is the decision coming into force immediately as it says to appoint you to be attached to the 121st Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This brigade was otherwise known or otherwise came to be known, did it not, as the Ruzhdi Selihu Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please. It is the battalion -- Ruzhdi Selihu Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yeah, my fault. Ruzhdi Selihu himself was killed, was he not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed on the 26th of July, 1998. Because of that the battalion took his name because he was the first martyr.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to suggest to you very clearly, Mr. Qeriqi, that brigades and battalions did not exist before well into August of 1998 at the earliest. Do you understand my question or suggestion?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree with it or do you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. I said also the day before yesterday that before this decision was taken Shukri Buja was there with me; I was his deputy. And from this date on, I knew of the existence of Brigade 121 as such and I was the commander of the Ruzhdi Selihu Battalion. From this time I took the minutes and everything that was linked with the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to try and be as clear about this as I possibly can be, Mr. Qeriqi, and I need your help. I'm suggest to you that there were no brigades and no battalions before, as I've described it, well into August of 1998. They simply didn't exist. The organisation of them had not happened. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. In that case we can move on to the last topic I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say something. This is why I brought with me this decision because at that time I was, as I should, be nominated properly as a battalion commander and I tried to do the proper organisation of the army that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The last thing I wanted to ask you about, please, is military police. Again, you gave us some evidence about this the day before yesterday and you may recollect you told us about their duties. Do you recollect telling us about all that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you without you asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. Well, we could proceed telepathically, but it may not help. What I want to do again is see if I can be clear about it, Mr. Qeriqi, and the formation of the military police. Again, I am suggesting -- or I suggest to you that the military police as an organisation within the KLA did not exist until later on beyond the summer of 1998. Now, do you understand what I'm suggesting to you, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by the end of summer; this I don't understand. Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Certainly. The military police, I suggest, did not exist as a group until sometime after the brigades and the battalions were formed, let's put it that way. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So when you told us yesterday that in your area you had two, three, or four military policemen, I suggest that if that's right they were not part of any military police unit that by then had been formed by the KLA because they did not get formed until later on in the year. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police I had, I said that they were there to take care of the soldiers and of the civilian population. When the decision -- as a battalion commander, when I made the decision from that time they were policemen at the level of the brigade. There was a special unit, that is, after the formation of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So it follows from the previous answers that you've given regarding formation of the brigades and so on, that that, what you've just described, could not have happened before the middle of August at the earliest. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember for sure, but it was around the time after I made the decision. The police were there in fact, but they were not under the command of the battalion; they were separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were not in a position as a battalion commander to organise or order anything until you became a battalion commander. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until that time, I worked with the -- with building the trenches, the bunkers as I explained earlier. And when there was a fighting somewhere, we fought of course. And it was also a normal thing for me not to command anything other than fight and build the positions, the bunkers. From Carraleve to Belince we had our positions. I trained the soldiers. This is what I did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you become aware -- my final question. Did you become aware that sometime much later in 1998 your old friend from Germany, Isak Musliu, Qerqizi, became a commander of the military police? Did you become aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Then in that case, I have no further questions. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I seem to be the travelling warrior in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Qeriqi.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I represent Haradin Bala and I have a number of questions to ask you and I hope that you're patient with me.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to start out with an understanding of what happened in the most general of senses when you had the interview with Mr. Whiting on April 23rd. Do you recall being at that interview?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall that when you were at that interview you started early in the morning, about 9.00, 9.30 in the morning and then you took a break after about three hours?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't take a three-hour break. To my recollection, and I don't think I forgot, I think we were there the entire day from 9.00 in the morning. And we didn't take a three-hour break; we made a five-minute break just for me to smoke a cigarette. Then we took a small lunch break. I had my meal for ten minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that was after you met for about three hours you took a break, they changed some tapes, and then you met with Mr. Whiting again in the afternoon. So there were actually two phases of your afternoon. You met in the morning, took a lunch break, and then you met in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small break, not longer than ten minutes. I was inside the entire day. I left that small room just to have my sandwich and then went back to the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you first -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The transcript is available and I believe that misstates the evidence, that the -- that it went for three hours. And I would draw counsel to the -- counsel's attention to the first page that the interview started at 9.23 and the first break occurred at 10.56. So after an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies. I had the time of 12.57 and -- the time is perhaps less critical, but I do -- I thank you so much for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you first met with Mr. Whiting, he told you that you had been called as a suspect. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was written on the summons that they brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. What I'm getting at is: When you were speaking with Mr. Whiting, when he first met with you he said: "In this investigation we're conducting at the moment you're considered a suspect."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I invite counsel to L010-9668.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what he told you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After he told you that, you -- Mr. Lehtinen, an investigator, spoke with you and he said to you: "We have decided to interview you and invite you as a suspect. In practice, don't let this disturb you at all."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I invite counsel to the next page, 9669.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember that being told to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I don't remember the entire interview, but it is true that I was questioned in the capacity of a suspect. Naturally I can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you took your morning break when you came back in the afternoon, Mr. Whiting further described to you your status as a suspect and was very clear with you about what your concerns should be and what your status was by saying the following, and once again I'm asking you whether or not you recall this particular statement being made to you by Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring counsel's attention to 109634 -- I apologise. I've lost the page; I'll find it in a second. That's 9696.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting said a series of things to you. He said: "And before you do, I want to say something. "Mr. Whiting: What you have to understand is that as we've told you, you are a suspect, but we are interested in your information primarily as a witness. We -- we are interested in hearing what you have to say as long as it's truthful. The way -- the best thing you can do for yourself is to tell the truth here. It's our -- of course it's difficult to talk about some of these things and certainly difficult to talk about your own role in them, but if we want you to be a witness, you have to be truthful otherwise we have to think about whether you are more of a suspect for us than a witness. So this is an opportunity for you to help yourself by telling the truth, even if it's difficult. Nobody is saying that you were the -- at the centre of this, but you did participate and you have to tell us that and you have to tell us why it happened." Do you recall Mr. Whiting discussing that with you, making that statement to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I don't remember this, but if it's written there in the minutes you read then he told me those things. In the beginning I told him that I will -- I was going to tell the truth and I told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... but a few moments later him telling you: "Nobody is here to criticise the good and important things you did and you've told us about some of the good and important things that you did that you should feel proud of. But to get credit for the good things that you've done you also have to take responsibility for the things that weren't so good that happened. And nobody is -- we want to know whether you -- whether you were there and you were involved or you were there and you were not involved and you saw it." Do you remember Mr. Whiting saying that to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably he said that, but for the moment I don't remember. Since it is written down, then he said that, but for the moment I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the course of the interview that you had with Mr. Whiting in April, the subjects that you discussed with him at that time included some of, if not all of the subjects that you've discussed with here during your testimony. And by that, I mean the subject of Mr. Xhemshiti. Do you remember discussing that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Also a discussion about some other people --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I ask that we go into private session for but a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the conclusion of the interview that you had with Mr. Whiting, Mr. Whiting invited you to come to The Hague to testify, saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I invite counsel's attention to page 9738.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- "Okay. If you were called to The Hague to testify in court, would you be willing to tell the Court everything you've told us today." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told him that I am able to say these things and -- meaning that I was not under pressure to come here by force. I was ready to come here and testify about things that I've done and about things that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since that discussion with Mr. Whiting back in April, have you received any notification orally - since Mr. Topolski asked you about anything that you may have received in writing - that your status had changed as a witness to come to The Hague to discuss matters?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in writing. No, I did not receive it in writing. The other person, Ole, or what was his name? I tend to forget his name. When we met with him he told me that after the investigation that they conducted, they found out that I was not a suspect. And this was in the end before I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to another subject if I could. If you could supply the gentleman with the map again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have the map there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... oh, there it is. Good. Now, could you with the pointer see if you could locate the village of Sedlare or Shale.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shale is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us approximately, if you know, what the distance is from Lapusnik to Sedlare or Shale?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might not be precise, but it could be 12 or 13 kilometres, around 12 or 13. 13 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the period of May through July, did you ever travel from Shale towards Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From May to July?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, when I went to join the fighting. Otherwise I did not go to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you on this particular -- in this particular path, is there an asphalt road or a direct road that goes from Shale to Lapusnik to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no asphalt road there. There's not one today and there wasn't one at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you help us and tell us, if you know, about how many different roads, if it's a matter of different roads, you would have to take to get from the area of Shale to Lapusnik? Is it one straight dirt road, a series of winding roads? Whatever it may be, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know because as I said I wasn't using those roads, but it is possible that they're not good roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to travelling from Klecka to Lapusnik, you indicated that you took that route by foot and it took you -- you weren't sure exactly how long but some two or three hours. Did you go by way of a road, a path, through fields? How were you able to get to Lapusnik on May 9th to fight?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used small paths, forest paths.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is Klecka on the same altitude as Lapusnik? Is it higher or lower than Lapusnik or the same altitude?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? Is it higher on the hill or -- I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's precisely what I mean. Is it higher on the hill?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this two days ago, that it has a very good geostrategic position for a war. It is on an upper position from all the other villages we've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you in a position to tell us about how much higher it is from all the other villages that you've mentioned so that we can get a better understanding of it's geostrategic position?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I'm not able to describe it really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Having walked from Lapusnik to Klecka after the battle on May 9th, could you tell us at that time were you walking up a hill?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, uphill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was it a steep hill?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we were really fit and it didn't seem a problem, but if I go now maybe it would be a problem for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What is the distance between Lapusnik and Klecka?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? How far they are apart?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, because as I said I did this journey just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, is it fair to say - and help me here - that the Berisa Mountains are part of the area in which Klecka is in?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I said that Klecka is upper in the hill. It is possible that Berisa is even higher because the radio was stationed there, Kosova Liv [phoen] radio, Free Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say the radio was stationed there, what radio was that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Free Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When did that radio station first come into existence, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. When it started to operate, as I said, I had already left for Tirana, but I heard it was operational there; to my knowledge it was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going back to the map again, do you see on the map the town of Bajice?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bajice is a village, not a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you point to it with your pointer.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, is there a way of getting to Bajice from the Lapusnik by way of an asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not possible. Bajice can never have an asphalt road. There's no asphalt road to Bajice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by any chance could you help us in this regard. Could you tell us what the distance is from Bajice to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I just might be mistaken here. Approximately when I spoke about Shale, Sedlare as you said, I said it was 12 or 13 kilometres based on Komorane. I wouldn't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Nekovce, could you point Nekovce out on that map, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was Nekovce an area that you were in between May and August of the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Shukri was in that area more than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you ever able to have contact with Shukri Buja when he was in Nekovce by way of radio during those summer months?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you, I never had a radio earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge were there other units that had radio communication abilities during the summer months?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We need the map no longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Part of your concern, I'm sure, as working with other soldiers was what would occur when anyone was wounded. True?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only my concern. It was the concern of all of us. This is quite natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. And in that regard, I'm hoping that you can be of some assistance. Do you know whether or not there was a hospital or a clinic in Lapusnik during the summer months?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What about the in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was one in Malisheve. Maybe there was one, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How about Shale? Was there a -- somewhere in Shale that someone could -- if they were wounded or otherwise needed medical attention get some medical attention there?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of those doctors by any chance?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ QERIQI [Resumed]
